div.p: This paper presents an algorithm for scheduling imprecise tasks to minimize maximum error and analyzes its performance through intensive simulation. The imprecise computation is used to manage transient overload of computation. Each task for imprecise systems consists of a mandatory part and an optional part that can be skipped when systems are overloaded The imprecise computation trades accuracy for meeting the deadline of tasks by skipping their optional parts. To increase accuracy for imprecise computation, we present a simple on-line scheduling algorithm that minimizes the maximum error. This algorithm executes mandatory parts of tasks first, then the optional parts in order to minimize maximum error. The proposed algorithm also increases schedulability by executing mandatory parts first. The proposed algorithm is simple and does not require any additional data structures such as the reservation list for maintaining mandatory parts.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In real-time systems, it is essential to finish tasks by their deadlines. The system works correctly only when tasks produce the results by their deadline. However, it is not possible for the system to meet the deadlines of some tasks when it is overloaded. Imprecise computation techniques [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8] were proposed to resolve transient overloads. In the imprecise computation model, each task can be divided into two parts, a mandatory part and an optional part. When system load is normal, the optional part is executed and the computation produces a 0-8186-9209-Xl98 $10.00 © 1998 IEEE 217 precise result. On overloaded conditions, however, all or portion of optional part is skipped to conserve system resources for the mandatory parts of other tasks. By skipping the optional part, the result of computation becomes imprecise. The imprecise computation sacrifices accuracy to meet the deadlines of mandatory parts. Many algorithms were presented to increase accuracy (minimize error) for imprecise computation [4,7,8]. Their objectives are minimizing one of folilowing error metrics: total error [7], maximum error [4,8].

We present a simple on-line scheduling algorithm that minimizes the maximum weighted error of tasks. The algorithm executes the mandatory parts of released tasks first and then the optiona� parts in order to minimize the maximmu error. The algorithm is simple and does not require any additional data structures such as the reservation list for maillltaining mandatory part. The algorithm also increases schedulability by executing mandatory part first, while producing comparable maximum errors with other algorithms.

div.head: Two-Level Scheduling
div.p: Many on-line schedule algorithms for imprecise systems were proposed. They try to satisfy criteria such as minimizing total error [7] or minimizing maximum error [3]. Without a priori knowledge of the parameters for tasks, we can hardly compute an optimal on-line schedule for imprecise tasks, minimizing total error or minimizing maximum weighted error.

Authors proposed a heuristic two-level scheduling policy [3] under the constraint that minimizes the largest weighted error. The top-level schedule, executed at every arrival time of a new task, computes the amount of processing time to be allocated for each task released by that instant. The minimizing algorithm was modeled as a linear optimization problem. The lower-level algorithm actually schedules the tasks. The actual execution time of a task is bounded by the processing time obtained by the top-level algorithm. When a new task arri ves, the amount of execution time computed in the top-level algorithm can be changed to minimize the largest weighted error.

div.head: On-line Algorithm to Minimize Maximum Weighted Error
div.p: Using the top-level algorithm, we determine the amount of processing time to be allocated to all tasks present in a system at that instant. However, we have many choices in selecting the low-level algorithm. The actual weighted errors incurred by tasks depend not only on the top-level algorithm but also on the lower-level algorithm.
In [3], Authors propose an algorithm to minimize maximum weighted error by modifying the on-line algorithm minimizing total error by Shih and Liu [7].
The algorithm by Shih and Liu [7] and the modified algorithm proposed in [3] work as follows.
• Shih&Liu algorithm to minimize total error: By reverse scheduling, the mandatory parts of all tasks are scheduled from the latest deadline to the current time.

Each mandatory part is scheduled by its deadline in the latest-ready-time-first order. This algorithm is suboptimal in terms of feasible schedules. When a task arrives, the mandatory part of the task is reserved using a reservation list [7].

• Modified Shih&Liu algorithm to mInImIZe maximum error: The modified Shih&Liu algorithm is same as the Shih&Liu algorithm except minimizing maximum error and considering the weights of tasks. When a task arrives, the algorithm makcs a rescrvation for the task. The amount of processing time to be allotted to task Tj with the earliest deadline is bounded by a value such that it reduces the largest weighted error as much as possible [3].

The major disadvantage of the above algorithms is as follows. When a new task arrives, it may not be possible to reserve intervals for its mandatory part, which makes the new task unschedulable and be rejected. However if the processor were used to execute mandatory parts, before executing optional parts in order to reduce the weighted errors, the reserved intervals could be available to execute the mandatory part of the new task. As the processor utilization increases, it is more probable that new arriving tasks are rejected.

Inspired by this problem, we consider a simple on-line algorithm to minimize the maximum weighted error of tasks. The proposed algorithm works as follows. The proposed algorithm is based on the EDF algorithm. It schedules the mandatory part of task with the earliest deadline first. If any processing time is available after executing the mandatory parts of all tasks that have been released, then the algorithm executes the optional parts of the released tasks in order to minimize maximum error. Since this algorithm executes the mandatory parts before any optional parts, it trades accuracy for schedulability. However, the simulation results show that our algorithm has a comparable accuracy (maximum error) while maintaining higher schedulability than the Shih&Liu algorithm minimizing total error and the modified Shih&Liu algorithm minimizing maximum error.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We presented a simple on-line algorithm for scheduling imprecise tasks to minimize ma.ximum error. The algorithm executes the mandatory parts of tasks first using the conventional EDF algorithm, then the optional parts in ordcr to minimize the maximum error. Our algorithm is simple and does not require any additional data structures such as a reservation list for the mandatory parts of tasks. Simulation results show that the maximum error generated by our algorithm is comparable with that of the modified Shih&Liu algorithm while increasing schedulability.
